source_caption:
Detachment (2011) is a psychological drama following Henry Barthes, a substitute teacher who moves from school to school while deliberately keeping an emotional distance from the people around him.
Henry enters a troubled high school where teachers struggle to control their classrooms and students face problems that extend far beyond their education. Although he initially tries to remain detached from the environment, his interactions with the students gradually begin breaking through the emotional walls he has built around himself.
As Henry connects with students dealing with neglect, loneliness, and difficult circumstances, he is forced to confront his own painful past. His ability to understand other people's struggles comes from experiences he has spent years trying to keep buried.
The film explores themes of isolation, education, trauma, compassion, identity, and the emotional distance people create to protect themselves. It shows how teachers can influence students while also revealing the personal struggles that educators may carry behind the classroom.
What makes Detachment compelling is its focus on the emotional reality of both teachers and students. Henry wants to remain an observer, but the people around him gradually make that distance harder to maintain.
More than just a movie about education, Detachment is a story about loneliness, human connection, and what happens when someone who has stopped caring begins to find a reason to connect again.
💬 How long can you stay detached when someone genuinely needs you?

source_details.synopsis: Detachment is a 2011 American psychological drama film directed by Tony Kaye and written by Carl Lund. Its story follows Henry Barthes, a high-school substitute teacher who becomes a role model to his students and others. It stars Adrien Brody, Marcia Gay Harden, Christina Hendricks, William Petersen, Bryan Cranston, Tim Blake Nelson, Betty Kaye, Sami Gayle, Lucy Liu, Blythe Danner and James Caan. Produced by Greg Shapiro, Carl Lund, Bingo Gubelmann, Austin Stark, Benji Kohn, and Chris Papavasiliou, the film was released on March 16, 2012, to mixed reviews.
